paragraphs: One-sentence judgment: A barber is not 'someone who just cuts it a bit shorter' but a shop position that provides cutting and styling and shaving and beard trimming services to customers: first asking clearly about the service and hairstyle the customer wants, cutting and trimming and styling hair with scissors and clippers and combs and blow dryers according to the customer's request or the current hairstyle, shampooing, shaving with a razor and trimming beards and mustaches with scissors, cleaning and disinfecting tools such as scissors and combs and clippers before and after cutting, cleaning the station and sweeping the floor, and recording the service and fees; people who only want to improvise by feel, are unwilling to first confirm the customer's request, and are unwilling to treat tool disinfection and station cleaning as part of the work are not suited.

Signals to keep exploring: you are willing to restate the service and hairstyle the customer wants before starting, can stay steady through the rhythm of close-range manual work and long periods of standing and receiving customers, will proactively check the symmetry and length baseline of the left and right and front and back outlines, are willing to clean and disinfect tools per procedure and record truthfully, and can first confirm and then adjust when a customer asks for changes or is dissatisfied.

Conditions for pausing investment first: you have not yet completed one full closed loop of 'consultation — cutting — shaving — disinfection — cleaning — recording' under any supervised conditions, or you can only express interest by 'liking styling'; also do not treat having cut hair for family and friends at home as proof that you can independently operate a razor and chemical perm and dye agents or independently take responsibility for venue sanitation and tool disinfection. Tool disinfection and skin barrier, chemical agent and perm and dye injury control, customer privacy and personal information handling, and practice and work authorization must follow the applicable jurisdiction and competent department and employer system with traceable records retained; this page does not provide any cutting, shaving, or chemical treatment operating instructions.

Education and practice licensing are two different tracks: O*NET lists 39-5011.00 as Job Zone Three (SVP 6.0 to <7.0); of the published education composition, 45% require a high school diploma or equivalent, 39% require a postsecondary certificate, and 12% require less than a high school diploma; the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook lists the typical entry education for this occupational group as 'postsecondary nondegree award', no related work experience requirement, and no on-the-job training, and notes that all states in the U.S. require barbers and cosmetologists to be licensed, usually requiring graduation from a state-approved barbering or cosmetology program and passing an examination. Education, vocational training, state practice license, employer appointment and shop authorization, and position authorization for tool disinfection and chemical agent use are different statuses and must be verified item by item by state and employer and position.

One sentence: This is a service position centered on first confirming the customer's request and then delivering steadily through close-range manual work and tool hygiene and receiving rhythms, with the core being cutting and styling and shaving and disinfection and recording, rather than an interest in hairstyles or an imagination about social media.

The work of barbers can be divided into three categories: cutting and shaving and styling services (asking about the service and hairstyle the customer wants; cutting and trimming hair with clippers and combs and hand-held blow dryers and scissors according to the customer's request or the current hairstyle; shampooing; shaving with a razor on the beard and neck and sideburn outlines after applying shaving cream; trimming beards and mustaches with scissors; putting a protective cape on the customer and pinning it; using chemical solutions and equipment as needed for curling or coloring or straightening; and providing face and neck and scalp massage); hygiene and safety and records (cleaning and disinfecting tools such as scissors and combs and clippers; cleaning the station and sweeping the floor; recording the services provided or collecting service fees on the register receipt; maintaining customer files and service and product use and fee records; and ordering supplies); and shop affairs and sales (undertaking clerical and administrative matters such as bookkeeping and accounts receivable and payable and hiring and supervision; recommending and selling hair care products and cosmetics; and offering care advice on hair problems). All three task categories are premised on first stopping to verify when the customer's request is unclear, the tool or agent status is unknown, or abnormal skin and health conditions are involved.

O*NET occupational identity and tasks: O*NET 39-5011.00 Barbers (2026 updated page, not marked Bright Outlook). The official duty is to provide barbering services, including cutting, trimming, shampooing, and styling hair, trimming beards, and giving shaves; there are 20 official tasks (18 core, 2 supplemental), with core task importance scores from 98 to 51 and the supplemental tasks at 58 and 45. Work activities are listed as 41 items on the detailed data page with importance scores, the highest being performing for or working directly with the public 88, establishing and maintaining interpersonal relationships 77, getting information 74, scheduling work and activities 73, organizing, planning, and prioritizing work 71, assisting and caring for others 70, thinking creatively 70, evaluating information to determine compliance with standards 68, updating and using relevant knowledge 68, training and teaching others 63, inspecting equipment, structures, or materials 62, communicating with people outside the organization 61, and performing general physical activities 61. Detailed work activities are 25 items (no scores). The task list describes the work of the group and does not mean every position performs all the tasks.

entries: Consultation and confirmation | Give the service a basis | Ask about the service and hairstyle the customer wants, and restate and confirm the length and outline baseline before starting.

Cutting and styling | Give the output a specification | Cut and trim with clippers and combs and hand-held blow dryers and scissors according to the customer's request or the current hairstyle, and adjust per customer feedback.
Shaving and beard trimming | Make the detail meet requirements | Apply shaving cream and shave the beard and neck and sideburn outlines with a razor, and trim beards and mustaches with scissors.

Tool disinfection and station cleaning | Keep risk controllable | Clean and disinfect tools such as scissors and combs and clippers, handle single-use items and potentially contaminated items, clean the station and sweep the floor.
Records and fees | Make the process traceable | Record the services provided or collect fees on the register receipt, and maintain customer files and service and product use and fee records.

Shop affairs and sales | Keep the business running | Undertake clerical and administrative matters such as bookkeeping and accounts receivable and payable and ordering and hiring and supervision, and recommend and sell hair care and cosmetic products within the authorized scope.

paragraphs: Work environment | 88% continually or almost continually use hands to handle and control or feel objects and tools, 78% continually or almost continually do repetitive motions, 84% continually or almost continually stand, 34% continually or almost continually bend or twist the body; 94% have telephone conversations every day, 85% have face-to-face discussions every day, 79% are in continual contact with others, 56% have very close physical proximity to others (near contact), 83% work indoors in an environmentally controlled setting every day; 32% are exposed to disease or infection every day, 23% are exposed to contaminants every day, 22% are exposed to minor burns or cuts or bites every day, 20% are exposed to distracting or uncomfortable noise every day, 16% are in hazardous conditions every day (78% never), 31% wear common protective or safety equipment every day; 53% sit less than half the time, 38% never sit; 88% never kneel, crouch, or crawl, 91% never climb ladders. Main equipment and tools | scissors and clippers and combs and razors and hand-held blow dryers, shampooing and styling and perm and dye equipment and chemical solutions, capes and single-use items, cleaning and disinfection supplies, register and appointment and customer file tools, personal protection (gloves and apron and face shield as the work requires). Task pace | 52% of typical workweeks exceed 40 hours, 36% are 40 hours, 12% are less than 40 hours; 94% have a regular schedule; 38% face time pressure every day; 65% consider the pace being determined by equipment speed not important at all; 67% have a lot of freedom in decisions, 69% have a lot of freedom in determining tasks and priorities and goals; 72% must make decisions every day. Collaborators | work with barbers and assistants and front desk colleagues in the same shop; 38% consider working with a work group or team extremely important (another 19% very important, 25% important), 31% have very high responsibility for the health and safety of others (another 25% high responsibility), 53% consider dealing with external customers or the public extremely important. Competition and pressure | 42% consider precision or accuracy extremely important (another 36% very important), 38% consider repeating the same tasks extremely important; 33% consider competition extremely fierce (another 36% highly competitive); 21% consider the consequences of error extremely serious (another 12% very serious, 21% serious); 16% deal with unpleasant or discourteous people every day, 58% encounter people with violent or physically aggressive behavior at least once a year but not every month, 13% are in conflict situations at least once a week but not every day. Compliance and safety | cutting and shaving and tool disinfection and station cleaning must conform to applicable hygiene and practice regulations; on the mainland China side the Regulations on the Administration of Public Place Sanitation provide that barbershops and beauty salons are covered venues, the operating unit is responsible for the sanitation management of its venue and must establish a sanitation responsibility system and conduct sanitation knowledge training and assessment for employees, and personnel who serve customers directly must hold a health certificate. Records and review | the service items and the tools and agents used, tool cleaning and disinfection handling, customer feedback and fees and anomalies need to be traceable; 42% consider precision or accuracy extremely important. Skills and training | O*NET lists this occupation as Job Zone Three (SVP 6.0 to <7.0); basic skills are mainly active listening 56 and speaking 53 and monitoring 44 and reading comprehension 44 and active learning 41 and critical thinking 41; transferable skills are mainly social perceptiveness 53, judgment and decision making 47, service orientation 47, coordination 41, time management 41, and persuasion 35; ability fields include speech recognition, imagination, problem sensitivity, speech clarity, and trunk strength; 52 abilities with Importance include arm-hand steadiness 72, near vision 69, oral comprehension 66, finger/manual dexterity 60 each, speech recognition/imagination 53 each, and problem sensitivity/speech clarity/trunk strength 50 each; problem sensitivity is identifying a problem, not necessarily solving it. 33 knowledge items include customer service 81, English 64, sales and marketing 62, education and training and public safety 61 each, law 54, and administration and chemistry 52 each. Work styles using Impact for 20 items: social orientation 75, dependability 68, cooperation 63, attention to detail 62, optimism 51, empathy 48, sincerity 46, self control 44, caution 33, innovation 32, integrity 32, stress tolerance 27; not a personality scale, individual threshold, or validity evidence. Entry and authorization | education and training do not equal a state practice license or employer appointment; on the U.S. side all states require a license, usually requiring completion of a state-approved program and passing an examination; on the mainland China side those who have not received sanitation knowledge training and assessment and obtained a health certificate must not serve customers directly. Industry and employers | the 2025 U.S. O*NET broad industry is other services (except public administration) 20% and other 80%; the OOH separately lists barbers as self-employed 80% and personal care services 20%. The levels and categories differ and cannot be added together; the OOH self-employed is a status, and the O*NET 'other' does not mean all other industries have been broken out; common employers are chain or independent shops, community barbershops, and hotel and resort and comprehensive hair and beauty establishments. Survey shares are not necessarily encountered by an individual, and the 70% not automated at all and 18% slightly automated are not an AI replacement rate. The current Regulations on the Administration of Public Place Sanitation (revised 2024-12-06) apply to barbershops and beauty salons; Article 3 requires customer utensils and so on to meet national hygiene standards, Articles 4/8 cover venue sanitation licenses, Article 6 makes the operating unit responsible for the sanitation system and employee sanitation knowledge training and assessment, Article 7 covers the health certificate for personnel who serve customers directly and the restriction before cure of diseases affecting public health, and Article 9 requires the operating unit to properly handle and report in a timely manner incidents endangering health. Venue certificates, health certificates, U.S. state occupational licenses, and employer position authority are different; this is not a uniform Chinese personal barbering license or a complete disinfection/stop-and-resume procedure.
Cutting and shaving and styling services

U.S. wage distribution: the 2025 BLS Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics (OEWS) displayed by O*NET give, under this occupation 39-5011.00, annual wage 10th percentile 28,600 USD, 25th percentile 31,570 USD, median 38,210 USD, 75th percentile 58,960 USD, 90th percentile 76,460 USD; hourly wage 10th percentile 13.75 USD, 25th percentile 15.18 USD, median 18.37 USD, 75th percentile 28.35 USD, 90th percentile 36.76 USD. The O*NET page does not state that these data are taken from another occupation, and they are under this occupational definition; the Pay section of the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook chapter separately lists the barber-specific May 2025 median hourly wage of 18.37 USD. The median does not equal the entry-level wage and does not constitute an income promise, and OEWS includes base pay, commissions, production bonuses, and tips, and excludes overtime premium, shift differential, and nonproduction bonuses, and so on; it excludes the self-employed and unregistered owners and partners and unpaid family workers. The OOH has 80% self-employed employment while OEWS wages exclude the self-employed, so the wage sample population cannot be treated as all employment.

Confirm the service and hairstyle the customer wants → shampoo and put on the protective cape → cut and trim and style per the customer's request or the current hairstyle → shave and trim the beard and sideburns → clean and disinfect tools and clean the station → record the service and fees and maintain customer files.

The 2022 Occupational Classification Code 4-10-03-02 hairdresser explicitly covers designing/trimming/making hairstyles, shampooing, hair cutting, dyeing and perming, hair setting, massage, razor face cleaning, hair care, and scalp care; it overlaps with U.S. Barbers in duties but the scope is not fully equivalent, and the same Chinese name does not imply mutual qualification recognition or a medical license. The precise national/city occupational wage is still missing; the 2025 China urban unit pre-tax annual average wage for resident services, repair, and other services: non-private 70,226 yuan, private 52,059 yuan. Referenced only when the actual unit's main activity belongs to this category, not the barber median, starting wage, percentile, or individual monthly take-home.
Hygiene and safety and records

U.S. 39-5011 barbers: 2025 employment 75,800, projected 78,300 in 2035, growth rounded to 3% over 2025—2035 (average), net increase rounded to 2,500, 6,900 openings per year on average. Openings include replacement demand, not a net increase, individual hiring probability, or AI causality. The same OOH chapter includes both the specific and combined values: 39-5010 combined 2025 employment 670,800, 719,200 in 2035, rounded 7%, 80,300 per year on average; barbers specifically 75,800→78,300 and 3%, wage 18.37 USD/hour, and barbers in the personal care services industry at a median of 18.26 USD/hour. The combined value cannot replace the specific one, nor can it be said that all values in that chapter are combined.

Confirm the tool and station status → clean and disinfect tools such as scissors and combs and clippers per procedure → replace or handle single-use items and potentially contaminated items → check the customer's skin and health condition and stop as needed → clean the station and sweep the floor → record disinfection and tool handling and anomalies.

The 2025 U.S. O*NET broad industry is other services (except public administration) 20% and other 80%; the OOH separately lists barbers as self-employed 80% and personal care services 20%. The levels and categories differ and cannot be added together; the OOH self-employed is a status, and the O*NET 'other' does not mean all other industries have been broken out. Work with barbers and assistants and front desk colleagues in the same shop; when tool disinfection and skin barrier, chemical agents and perm and dye injuries, customer privacy and personal information, or the scope of practice and work authorization are involved, act per the applicable jurisdiction and competent department and employer system, do not decide on one's own, and stop and report when the customer's skin or health condition is abnormal or the tool or agent status is unknown.

Barbers focus on cutting and shaving and beard trimming and styling; hairstylists and hair designers and cosmetologists focus on comprehensive hairstyling and chemical services; manicurists and pedicurists focus on nail services; skincare specialists focus on facial and skin care; shampooers focus on shampooing and assisting with washing and preparation; theatrical makeup artists focus on performance and film makeup; massage therapists focus on soft tissue massage and body care. Adjacent occupations share the personal service setting and customer communication and hygiene fundamentals, but the core output, tools, and authorization requirements differ.
A reviewable service and hygiene and fee record

Complete cutting and styling and shaving per the customer's request, and leave a record stating the service items and the tools and agents used, the tool cleaning and disinfection handling, customer feedback and revisions, fees and anomalies and the parts that remain uncertain, so that shop colleagues and the supervisor can review from it.
Service and hygiene and fee records

The object is the customer's hair and beard and scalp and skin, tools such as scissors and clippers and combs and razors and blow dryers, and shampoo and styling and perm and dye products; the basis is the customer's explicit request, the employer's and venue's hygiene and disinfection procedures, and the applicable practice and venue hygiene regulations.

Barbers (O*NET 39-5011.00 on the U.S. side, Barbers) provide barbering services, including cutting, trimming, shampooing, and styling hair, trimming beards, and giving shaves. The original official duty text is 'Provide barbering services, such as cutting, trimming, shampooing, and styling hair; trimming beards; or giving shaves.'; O*NET lists 20 official tasks (18 core, 2 supplemental); core tasks include cleaning and disinfecting scissors and combs and clippers and other tools (importance 98), cutting and trimming hair with clippers and combs and hand-held blow dryers and scissors according to the customer's request or the current hairstyle (97), asking the customer about the service and hairstyle they want (97), cleaning the station and sweeping the floor (94), putting the protective cape on the customer and pinning it (94), applying shaving cream and shaving the beard and neck and sideburn outlines with a razor (89), recording the service or collecting fees on the register receipt (85), trimming beards and mustaches with scissors (84), undertaking clerical and administrative matters such as bookkeeping and accounts receivable and payable and hiring and supervision (79), maintaining customer files and recording the service and product use and fees for each visit (77), keeping up to date on the latest hairstyles and hair care techniques (75), and shampooing (73); supplemental tasks include analyzing and identifying hair problems with microscopes and testing equipment or an outside laboratory (58), and measuring and fitting and adjusting wigs (45). This occupation is in Job Zone Three (SVP 6.0 to <7.0) in the U.S. This page does not constitute cutting, shaving, or chemical treatment operating instructions.
Consultation — cutting — shaving — disinfection — cleaning — recording

Confirm the customer's request and service scope → shampoo and cape and prepare tools → cut and style and adjust per customer feedback → shave and trim the beard and sideburns → clean and disinfect tools and clean the station → record the service and fees and anomalies.
A reviewable service and disinfection and tool handling record
The service items and the tools and agents used, tool cleaning and disinfection and single-use item handling, customer feedback and revisions, fees and anomalies, and the parts that remain uncertain.
Self and shop colleagues and the supervisor

Cutting and styling and shaving conclusions are undertaken by the person according to job duties; when tool disinfection and skin barrier, chemical agents and perm and dye, abnormal customer skin or health conditions, and the determination of hygiene responsibility and the scope of practice are involved, they are made by personnel with the corresponding duties and authorization per the applicable jurisdiction and competent department and employer system, and work must stop and report when the customer's condition is abnormal or the work exceeds the person's scope of practice.
Education and practice licensing

O*NET lists 39-5011.00 as Job Zone Three (SVP 6.0 to <7.0); among the educational attainment the page publishes, 45% require a high school diploma or equivalent, 39% require a postsecondary certificate, and 12% require less than a high school diploma. The BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook lists the typical entry-level education for this occupational group as a postsecondary nondegree award, with no related work experience and no on-the-job training required, and notes that every U.S. state requires barbers and cosmetologists to be licensed, usually requiring graduation from a state-approved barbering or cosmetology program and passing an examination. The O*NET training page shows 1,280 related training programs nationwide (Barbering / Barber, Hair Styling, Salon Management, and Cosmetology, Barber / Styling, and Nail Instructor fields), and the certification page shows that no unified national certification is registered for this occupation. On the mainland China side, employer-provided pre-job training and on-the-job mentoring predominate, and practitioners must meet the requirements of the Regulations on the Administration of Public Place Hygiene for hygiene knowledge training and health certificates for workers.
Do not substitute for one another

Education, occupational training, state practice licensure, employer hiring and shop authorization, and job-level authorization for tool disinfection and chemical product use are different statuses: education and completion of training do not confer a practice license or authorization to handle tools and chemical products; each must be verified item by item according to the state (or territory), employer, and position.

Verify at least six items before starting: the occupational definition and employer entity (O*NET 39-5011.00 is the U.S. definition); education and occupational training; state practice license and renewal requirements; the scope of employer hiring and in-shop authorization (including whether it covers razors, chemical permanent waving and dyeing, and beard trimming); venue hygiene, tool disinfection, and worker health management requirements; and the employment arrangement and compensation basis (hourly wage or commission, tips, and self-employment).
Occupational definition

The U.S. side is O*NET 39-5011.00 (Barbers); its wage, employment, and industry data are for this occupational definition, and the page does not state that they are taken from another occupation, and O*NET does not mark it as Bright Outlook. The corresponding chapter of the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook is the combined “Barbers, Hairstylists, and Cosmetologists” definition, which cannot be treated as a barber-only definition. On the mainland China side, this page has not obtained a precise national occupational wage distribution for barbers, so the boundary of no data that can be safely used is retained and is not replaced by industry or recruitment data; when comparing, first identify whether a position belongs to a chain or independent shop, a community barbershop, or a hotel, resort, and comprehensive hair and beauty establishment.
Education and practice licensure pathway

On the U.S. side, educational attainment is mainly a high school diploma or equivalent (45%, with another 39% holding a postsecondary certificate and 12% less than a high school diploma); the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook lists the typical entry-level education as a “postsecondary nondegree award” and notes that all states require licensure, usually requiring completion of a state-approved program and passing an examination; O*NET lists 1,280 related training programs (Barbering / Hair Styling / Salon Management fields). In mainland China, employer-provided pre-job training and on-the-job mentoring predominate, and practitioners must meet the requirements of the Regulations on the Administration of Public Place Hygiene for hygiene knowledge training and health certificates; specific education and experience requirements are set by the employer.
Practice and task authorization

Cutting, shaving, and tool disinfection must be carried out in accordance with the applicable jurisdiction, the competent authority, and employer procedures; where razor use, chemical permanent waving and dyeing and chemical products, and the handling of abnormal skin or health conditions are involved, this must be done within the scope of the practice license and shop authorization and escalated according to procedure. On the U.S. side, practice licensure is administered by each state and usually requires completion of a state-approved program and passing an examination; the O*NET certification page shows that no unified national certification is registered for this occupation. On the mainland China side, the Regulations on the Administration of Public Place Hygiene require operating units to train and assess workers in hygiene knowledge and require personnel who serve customers directly to hold a health certificate on duty; verify the training and authorization process before starting, and do not infer it directly from education or experience.
Venue hygiene and tool disinfection

The work environment and tools must meet applicable hygiene and safety requirements (cleaning and disinfecting tools, handling disposables and contaminated items, cleaning workstations and floors, ventilation and lighting, and protection against prolonged standing and repetitive motions). O*NET work context shows 88% spend time continuously or almost continuously using hands to handle, control, or feel objects and tools, 78% continuously or almost continuously make repetitive motions, 84% continuously or almost continuously stand, 94% have telephone conversations every day, 85% have face-to-face discussions every day, 56% work very close (within touching distance) to others, 32% are exposed to disease or infections every day, 23% are exposed to contaminants every day, and 22% are exposed to minor burns, cuts, bites, or stings every day; this page does not constitute work instructions or disinfection step instructions.
Shifts and working hours

Work context shows that for 52% the typical workweek exceeds 40 hours, 36% work 40 hours, and 12% work less than 40 hours; 94% have a regular schedule; 38% face time pressure every day; 33% consider competition extremely fierce and 36% consider it highly fierce. The BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook notes that most practitioners work full time and that part-time work is also common, and that schedules often include evenings and weekends. When comparing positions, write the employment arrangement, commission, tips, self-employment arrangements, and overtime rules into the written terms.
Continuing training and review

Hairstyles, tools, and chemical products change relatively quickly; O*NET lists 7 software skills marked as hot technologies (Microsoft Office, Facebook, Linux, Microsoft Excel, Microsoft PowerPoint, Microsoft Windows, Microsoft Word), of which only Microsoft Office has a published occurrence rate below 1%; basic skills are led by active listening 56, speaking 53, monitoring 44, and reading comprehension 44; transferable skills are led by social perceptiveness 53, judgment and decision making 47, service orientation 47, coordination 41, and time management 41; work styles include social orientation and dependability. Confirm continuing education and license renewal arrangements and the shop authorization and review mechanism before starting.

All six directions share a background of personal service settings, customer communication, and basic hygiene knowledge, but their work objects, deliverable results, and practice and authorization requirements differ; the same shop reception or service experience cannot be directly converted into a license or task authorization for another direction, and this page only compares differences in duties under public definitions.

The basis for comparison is the official occupational description of O*NET 39-5011.00 and the related occupations list on the O*NET page, as well as the adjacent occupation relationships indicated in the routing materials; an adjacent relationship only describes proximity of duties and does not mean that licenses, authorizations, or positions are interchangeable.

The table below compares barbers with five adjacent directions along the same set of dimensions: occupational direction, core work and output, key differences, and which option better suits each preference.

Hairdressers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists focus on comprehensive hairstyling and chemical services, typically covering a broader range including cutting, permanent waving, dyeing, and beauty treatments; barbers focus on cutting, shaving, beard trimming, and styling.

If you prefer comprehensive hairstyling, chemical services, and beauty treatments, compare hairdressers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists first; if you prefer focusing on cutting, shaving, and beard trimming, barbering is suitable.
Design and deliver comprehensive hairstyling and chemical services, with output mainly hairstyle results and service records.
Barbers and hairdressers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists
Manicurists and pedicurists focus on shaping, decorating, and caring for nails and typically do not work on hair or beards; barbers focus on cutting and styling hair and beards.
If you prefer nail services, compare manicurists and pedicurists first; if you prefer cutting hair and beards, barbering is suitable.
Shape, decorate, and care for nails, with output mainly nail results and service records.
Barbers and manicurists and pedicurists

Skincare specialists focus on facial and skin care and beauty treatments and typically do not perform cutting or shaving; barbers focus on cutting and shaving hair and beards, and skin care is only an incidental service.
If you prefer facial and skin care, compare skincare specialists first; if you prefer cutting and shaving, barbering is suitable.
Deliver facial and skin care treatments, with output mainly skin care results and customer records.
Barbers and skincare specialists

Shampooers focus on shampooing and assisting with washing and preparation and typically do not independently make cutting and shaving decisions; barbers handle the complete service loop from consultation to cutting to shaving to charging.
If you prefer shampooing, preparation, and assistance, compare shampooers first; if you prefer to handle the complete cutting and shaving loop, barbering is suitable.
Perform shampooing, washing, preparation, and assistance, with output mainly washing and preparation records.
Barbers and shampooers

Stage makeup artists focus on performance, film, and stage makeup and styling, and their work object is the makeup look and character image rather than everyday hairstyles; barbers focus on everyday cutting, shaving, and styling.
If you prefer performance and film makeup, compare stage makeup artists first; if you prefer everyday cutting and shaving, barbering is suitable.
Complete makeup and styling according to performance or shooting requirements, with output mainly makeup and styling results.
Barbers and stage makeup artists

Massage therapists focus on soft tissue massage and body care and require a separate practice and training pathway; barbers focus on hair and beard services, and massage is usually only an incidental service.
If you prefer body massage and soft tissue care, compare massage therapists first; if you prefer hair and beard services, barbering is suitable.
Perform soft tissue massage and body care according to a plan, with output mainly session records and customer feedback.
Barbers and massage therapists

Conclusion: the basis for choosing a direction is the work object, deliverable results, and practice requirements, not whether both work in personal service settings; after choosing a direction, verify item by item the training, licensing, and task authorization requirements of the target direction.

entries.answer: Provide barbering services to customers: asking customers what services and hairstyles they want; using clippers, combs, a hand-held hair dryer, and scissors to cut and trim hair and style it according to customer requirements or the current hairstyle; shampooing; applying shaving cream and shaving the beard, neck, and sideburn outlines with a razor; trimming the beard and mustache with scissors; cleaning and disinfecting tools such as scissors, combs, and clippers; cleaning workstations and sweeping floors; recording the services provided or fees charged on the cash register slip; and maintaining customer files and ordering supplies.

entries.answer: Mainly tool disinfection and skin barrier (cross-infection), chemical product and permanent waving and dyeing injuries, customer privacy and personal information leaks, repetitive motion and prolonged standing injuries, out-of-control customer and disinfection records, and unclear hygiene responsibility and scope of practice; the control method is to act in accordance with the applicable jurisdiction, the competent authority, and employer procedures, clean and disinfect tools and separate disposables, use chemical products according to product instructions and perform a skin assessment first, and adjust the workstation and rotate services while reporting discomfort early.

entries.answer: Verify under six categories: education; occupational training; state practice license and renewal; shop pre-job training; shop task authorization (including whether it covers razors, chemical permanent waving and dyeing, and beard trimming); and hygiene and disinfection and customer information protection training. On the U.S. side, every state requires licensure, usually requiring completion of a state-approved program and passing an examination (BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook); on the mainland China side, the Regulations on the Administration of Public Place Hygiene require operating units to provide hygiene knowledge training and assessment for workers and require personnel who serve customers directly to hold a health certificate on duty. subject.summary: Barbers provide haircutting services to customers: asking about and confirming the service and hairstyle the customer wants, cutting and trimming and styling hair with scissors and clippers and combs and blow dryers, shampooing, shaving with a razor and trimming beards and mustaches with scissors, cleaning and disinfecting tools such as scissors and combs and clippers, and maintaining customer files and fee records. On the U.S. side this corresponds to O*NET 39-5011.00 (Barbers), in Job Zone Three (SVP 6.0 to <7.0); the wage and employment and industry data are all under this occupational definition, and the O*NET page does not state that they are taken from another occupation (the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook chapter is the combined 'Barbers, Hairstylists, and Cosmetologists' definition, marked separately on this page). On the mainland China side this page obtained no public occupational entry and national wage distribution precisely corresponding to barbers, retaining the 'no safely usable data' boundary, not substituting industry or hiring data, nor treating the Chinese page language as an equivalent Chinese occupation or a wage mapping.
